parts.title: A systematic review of recent efforts to help patients leave the hospital and move between care settings, seen through patients' own experiences
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Aim

We wanted to bring together what recent studies found about how efforts to improve three parts of care affect patients' experiences. The three parts are care coordination (making sure different doctors and services work together for one person), discharge support (helping patients get ready to leave the hospital and understand what comes next), and care transitions (helping patients move smoothly from one care setting to another, such as from hospital to home).

Method

We carried out a systematic review, which is a careful, planned search of published research. We searched six scientific databases and five specialist journals. We also used "snowballing": we followed the references of the studies we found and looked for similar studies. To be included, a study had to be published in English between 2015 and 2023. It had to focus on improving care coordination, discharge support or transitional care, and it had to measure patients' experiences as a main result, using a standardized measure (one that is used in the same way across many places). Two reviewers worked independently to decide which studies qualified and to judge how well each study was done.

Results

We first checked 1240 papers, and 16 made it into the review. Seven studies focused on care coordination. Three of these were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), which are experiments where patients or clinics are assigned to a new approach or to usual care by chance. These studies added extra support, such as coaching to help clinics improve, or changes tailored to vulnerable groups of patients. They took place in Patient-Centered Medical Homes (clinics that organize care around the patient) or in other primary care settings. Compared with standard care or simpler supports, such as a quality-improvement tool, the results were mixed or neutral.

Eight studies, including three RCTs, focused on extra discharge support. This included teaching patients, for example with "teach back" (where a patient repeats back what they were told to check they understood), and follow-up by telephone. These studies also found mixed or neutral results for patients' experiences, and they had more serious risks of bias, meaning flaws in how the studies were done that could make the results less trustworthy. One practical trial tested a transitional care program that used a "navigator" to guide patients. It found statistically significant changes only for patients without health insurance, and only in one measure of patient experience. (A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone.) This trial also had trouble making sure the program was carried out exactly as planned.

Conclusion

Extra support for care coordination, discharge teaching and follow-up after discharge had mixed or neutral effects on patients' experiences of care, compared with standard care or simpler ways of improving care. We need more evidence on how to improve patients' experiences with discharge support and with help moving between care settings.
parts.introduction_first: How patients experience care is a key part of what makes healthcare good. It shows how much care is shaped around the person receiving it, and it helps guide efforts to improve quality [1–3]. By "patient experience" we mean how patients felt about important parts of their care. Examples include how well doctors communicated, whether patients were involved in decisions, whether they could get appointments in time, and how well care was coordinated and discharge planning worked across different settings. Discharge planning is the work of getting a patient ready to leave the hospital. These parts matter because care is often broken into pieces, with different doctors and services not working together well [1].
parts.conclusion:
Conclusion

Extra support for care coordination and discharge support had mixed or neutral results for improving patients' experiences of care, compared with standard care or simpler supports. We cannot draw firmer conclusions because many studies had a substantial risk of bias, and because studies often did not compare different ways of improving care. This is especially true for the studies on extra discharge support, which were also usually carried out at a single center. The studies on extra care coordination that covered several sites were also limited, because they all took place within one health system, network or organization. That makes it harder to know whether the results apply to other organizations and ways of delivering care.

Finally, future studies should look at how transitional care programs affect patients' experiences. They should also make sure the programs are carried out exactly as planned, and use adaptive designs, which let a study change its plan as it learns from what it finds. We need stronger evidence on how efforts to improve health services affect patients' experiences, especially through better discharge support and better help moving between care settings.
parts.introduction_rest:
Several systematic reviews have brought together earlier research on this question. They found that when patients have better experiences of care, they are more likely to follow their treatment, and both patients and health systems tend to do better [4–7]. For example, one recent systematic review looked at standardized measures of patient experience. It found that patients who scored better on these measures also reported better physical and mental health. They were also admitted to hospital less often and for shorter stays, and they went to the emergency room fewer times [4]. Improving patients' experiences has also become a goal in its own right for efforts to improve quality. The idea is to make care more centered on the person receiving it [8, 9].

Many health systems now pay providers partly based on the value of the care they give, and this includes patients' experience scores. In the United States, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) has created the Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems (CAHPS) surveys and quality measures. These are widely used to track, publicly report and compare how well providers do on patients' experiences [10]. In some programs that pay providers for good performance, the US Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services uses CAHPS scores to work out payment rewards [11]. Several other countries require providers to keep track of patients' experiences and to improve them [12, 13].

Overall, health systems, organizations and the doctors and staff who work directly with patients all face pressure to build up organized ways of improving patients' experiences [14]. This pressure can come from rules about quality, from rewards for good value, or from the market, for example the need to keep patients loyal. It includes improving care coordination and discharge support [15, 16].

There are several ways to make care less broken into pieces, help it flow more smoothly over time, and stop patients from being admitted to hospital again. Examples include supported discharge (care that is coordinated as a patient moves from the hospital back to their home), case management programs (where a worker helps a patient manage their care and needs), transitional care services, the use of care coordinators, and ways of organizing care such as Patient-Centered Medical Homes [17, 18]. Systematic reviews have looked at how well these efforts work, and many have been shown to help with a range of results for patients' health, their quality of life and the health system [17–20]. For example, efforts to help patients move from hospital to home can work well at reducing readmission, meaning being admitted to hospital again. This is especially true when they start in the hospital and carry on in the community, through follow-up by telephone or other telehealth (care delivered by phone or video) or through planned home visits [18, 19, 21].

However, we found no systematic review that looked at how care coordination, discharge support or transitional care affect patients' experiences of care. A recent overview of systematic reviews on care coordination found that patients' experiences were rarely studied or reported as a result of these efforts [22].

In this paper, we aim to bring together recent research (from 2015 to 2023) on how care coordination, discharge support and transitional care affect patients' experiences. We focus on experiences measured by formal patient-reported measures, which are surveys that ask patients themselves how they felt about their care.
parts.methods:
Materials and methods

How we planned the review

Before we began, we registered a plan for this systematic review in PROSPERO, a public register of review plans (registration number CRD42022358337). The plan set out to bring together recent research written in English about efforts to improve health services that aim to make patients' experiences of care better. In this paper, we focus on how three kinds of effort affect patients' experiences: extra care coordination, discharge support and transitional care. To write the review report, we followed a widely used set of guidelines called the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PIRSMA). The checklist is in the S1 Appendix.

Which studies we included

We included three kinds of study. The first was controlled trials, where a group gets the new effort and another group gets usual care so the two can be compared. The second was observational studies that followed patients over time and included a comparison group. The third was "pre-post" studies, which compare the same patients before and after the effort. Every study had to include more than 30 participants. We left out studies that explored people's views and experiences in words rather than numbers (qualitative studies), studies that compared different countries, and any study that did not measure how patients' experiences changed.

To be included, a study also had to meet three more conditions. Its full text had to be available. Improving patients' experiences had to be one of its two main results it set out to measure. And it had to report statistics that test whether the effort made a difference, such as p-values. A p-value tells us how often a gap at least this large would turn up by chance alone if the effort really had no effect.

For patients' experiences, we included studies that used standardized, number-based measures. These included validated surveys (surveys that have been tested and shown to measure what they are meant to), single questions from those surveys, or groups of questions combined into one score. We also included surveys that were collected outside the hospital and used routinely across many providers, including surveys used to decide how much money providers are paid for the care they give (value-based reimbursement). We left out studies that measured patients' experiences only with tools that were not standardized, were qualitative, or had not been validated. We also left out measures that were not reported by the patients themselves, such as measures based on what observers watched. We did not bring together results for any measure other than patients' experiences of care.

For participants, we included health systems, organizations, providers, networks, care settings or service units, and any health professionals or staff. We left out efforts to improve care that were carried out only by students or doctors and nurses still in training. The people who gave feedback about their experience could be the patient, a family member or informal caregiver, or any of these people speaking on the patient's behalf.

For where and when the studies took place, we did not limit the countries. However, we only included articles written in English and published in 2015 or later. This was to capture recent efforts that respond to the recent focus, and the money-based rewards, on improving patients' experiences of care. For example, in the US, payments that included patients' experience scores did not start until 2013 [23].

In this review, we only included efforts to improve health services that focused on one of three areas. Care coordination means organized plans, made by an organization, a service line or a service unit, to deal with care that is broken into pieces and to help care stay connected over time [22]. Discharge support means teaching patients to get ready to leave the hospital, and/or teaching them or following up with them after they leave, either in person or by telephone, video or other online means [18]. Transitional care means a limited set of actions, carried out over a short time and with help from others, to make sure care stays connected or coordinated as patients move between different settings or levels of care [24]. Transitional care often gives patients a single point of contact, to make it easier to get services, to communicate and to coordinate care [25].

How we searched for studies

We searched six scientific databases: PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL, EconLit, PsycINFO, DOAJ and Scopus. We used a mix of everyday words and the special search terms each database uses, chosen to match our rules for which studies to include. We limited the search to English-language articles published after January 2015. The S2 Appendix shows the exact search for each database. We first ran the searches in December 2022 and ran them again in January 2024.

We also searched four journals directly: the Patient Experience Journal, the Journal of Patient Experience, Medical Care and Health Expectations. We searched the journal NEJM Catalyst Innovations in Care Delivery from January 2020 onward, because that is when it started checking papers with other experts before publishing them (peer review). We chose these journals because our first database searches often turned up papers in them. Finally, we used snowballing. We followed the references of the studies we had included, and we looked for similar studies in PubMed. We also checked the reference lists of similar systematic reviews, such as those we found through our searches.

How we chose studies

Two reviewers worked independently to check each study. The first reviewer was TJ. The second reviewer was DL, JS or MZ. They first read each study's title and abstract, and then read the full text to see whether it met our rules for inclusion. A third reviewer, AD, helped settle any disagreements.

How we recorded information from each study

Our research team built a form for recording information from each study. It covered the study's features and setting, the measures of patients' experiences and how they were scored, the effort being tested, how the study analyzed its data, and the results for patients' experiences of care. The first author (TJ) filled in the form first, and a second author (BS) checked it. After that, we went through any entries that raised questions until we agreed on them. The S3 Appendix gives the agreed information for each study we included.

How we judged the quality of each study

TJ and BS judged the quality of each study independently. For controlled trials, we used the risk of bias rules suggested by the Cochrane group for reviews of how care is organized and delivered (Effective Practice and Organization of Care, or EPOC) [26]. For pre-post studies and observational studies that measured or compared the effects of efforts to improve health services, we used the quality-checking tools of the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute [27].

As we had planned in our review plan, we did not give the studies an overall grade for how strong their evidence was, based on their design. Our review covers a wide range of efforts to improve health services or quality, settings, measures and study designs. So it is "configurative": it describes and compares the studies, rather than "aggregative", which would mean combining their results into one overall number. We made a table of the agreed risk of bias for each study's setting and design, based on the checklist method used for that kind of study. The full details of these checks are in the S4 Appendix.

How we analyzed the results

We grouped and summarized the results in three main categories: 1) care coordination, 2) discharge support and 3) transitional care. Within each category, we made a table of each study's methods and judged its risk of bias. We then brought together the efforts and their findings, first ordering the studies by type of design (starting with randomized controlled trials) and then by publication date within each design. Because our review describes and compares studies rather than combining their results, and because the efforts and study settings were so different, we did not carry out a meta-analysis, which is a statistical method for combining the numbers from many studies into one overall result.
parts.results:
Results

We checked 1240 different papers. Of these, 143 full papers were judged close enough to be worth reading in full, and 16 of those made it into the review [15, 16, 28–40]. The main reason a full paper was left out was that it did not measure the effect of the program using statistics that test whether a difference could be due to chance.

Seven of the 16 papers focused on extra care coordination support, beyond what Patient-Centered Medical Homes (clinics that organize care around the patient) normally provide. Eight focused on extra discharge support. These studies tested better patient teaching, a redesigned way of getting patients ready to leave the hospital, follow-up by telephone, or a mix of these. One paper focused on transitional care, which is help moving between care settings.

All the studies took place in several PCMHs or other primary care clinics, all within a network or integrated health system in the US. These were the Veterans' Health Administration (VHA) [34–36], a statewide PCMH network [37], Federally Qualified Health Centers [38], a Safety Net Medical Homes' Initiative [40], and primary care clinics linked to universities [39].

Three studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of help with improvement projects at each clinic. The most recent of these, at the VHA, had the fewest risks of bias (Table 1). It used quality-improvement help, such as coaching by improvement experts from a central team, to support each clinic in using a care-coordination improvement toolkit, beyond sharing the toolkit internally (the comparison). Both groups showed improvements in patients' experiences, but the group that received the extra coaching, which took more resources, showed no significant benefit [36].

Another RCT looked at extra care coordination for patients at high risk of being admitted to hospital, beyond standard PCMH care (the comparison). It found improvements in 2 of the 6 care coordination items measured from patients' experiences [35]. The third RCT encouraged clinics to choose high-value care coordination quality-improvement goals, beyond standard quality-improvement help (the comparison), and found mixed results [37]. These RCTs had risks of bias, such as the program possibly spreading to the comparison clinics [35] and differences in which clinics took part [37].

Among the other types of study, one non-randomized trial looked at nurses giving extra care coordination and navigation support to socially vulnerable patients, beyond a PCMH model (the comparison). It found no statistically significant differences between the groups (p = 0.07) [38]. Finally, three observational studies found mixed results and had substantial risks of bias (Table 1). These were a study that tailored the PCMH model to homeless patients [34], a study of practice transformation tailored to safety-net clinics [40], and a study of a learning collaborative [39].

Of the three RCTs, two focused on teaching patients at discharge using teach back, either after checking health literacy [28] or as part of discharge support in the patient's own language, with several kinds of help and telephone follow-up [29]. None of these programs led to better experience results than standard care. The third RCT tested a web-based surgical patient education tool for instructions before surgery and for follow-up, and found improvements in the overall experience score [30]. However, all the RCTs had risks of bias, such as being a single-center study [28–30], having short follow-up [29, 30], or not correcting for multiple comparisons [28–30] (Table 3).

We found two non-randomized trials. One tested ReEngineered Discharge for three patients a day, with nurses choosing patients as complex cases [16]. The other tested teach-back discharge teaching by nurses [33]. Both improved some patient experience items, such as how well patients were given information.

An observational study with historical controls looked at telephone follow-up after hospital discharge, with possible plans to fix problems or rescue resources (for example, a same-day clinic appointment) [15]. The program group had higher percentages of top-box scores (the highest possible score on a patient experience item) than the comparison group for 5 of the 11 items. Several risks of bias applied to these three studies (Table 3), including the program possibly spreading and analyses that did not take other factors into account.

Finally, we included two before-and-after studies. One used teach back and other changes to discharge [31], and the other used pharmacist-led discharge teaching and follow-up [32]. These gave either positive or mixed results: top-box percentages improved, but percentile ranks did not improve compared with other providers. Besides having no comparison group, these studies had several substantial risks of bias (Table 3), which limits what we can conclude.

c) Transitional care program

One practical clinical trial tested a transitional care program that helped patients move from hospital to the community, with support from community health workers and peer coaches [41]. Table 5 describes how the study was done, where it took place, its risks of bias, the program, and the results.

The navigator program did not improve patients' experiences, judged by the differences between the groups in changes in information support. However, when the results were split into subgroups, patients without health insurance showed greater improvements in information support. The program may not have been carried out exactly as planned, and the measure used may not have captured the full range of what the program offered (Table 5). These may have contributed to the results that were not statistically significant.

Discussion

Our review fills a gap in what is known about how care coordination, discharge support and help moving between care settings affect standardized measures of patients' experiences. Efforts to improve health services, such as extra support or changes tailored to vulnerable groups of patients, gave mixed or no improvement in patients' experiences of care coordination or discharge, compared with usual care or simpler ways of improving care.

Seven studies found this for extra support for care coordination. These studies gave the support to Patient-Centered Medical Homes (clinics that organize care around the patient) or to other primary care practices. Three of them were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that covered several sites. Eight studies found the same for extra discharge support. This support included teaching patients, a reengineered discharge (a discharge process that has been redesigned to work better), and/or follow-up by telephone or other help moving between care settings. Taken together, these studies had a substantial risk of bias. Finally, one transitional care program used a navigator to guide patients. It did not improve patients' experiences of the information they received. However, when the results were split into groups, patients without health insurance showed greater improvements in the information they received.

We found several risks of bias across the studies we reviewed, in how they were designed. These risks limit how far the findings hold up within each study and how far they apply to other places. The studies on extra discharge support were usually carried out at a single center. Even the studies on extra care coordination that covered several sites all took place within one network or organization. So we do not know how the findings apply elsewhere.

For example, the study with the lowest risk of bias found that a type of support for Patient-Centered Medical Homes, which took more resources, did not do better than simply sharing a quality-improvement tool. Both were tested for how much they improved patients' experiences of care coordination. But that knowledge comes from a study within the Veterans Health Administration (VHA), the US government's health system for veterans, and it applies directly to the VHA. The VHA has set up its own organized programs, studies and activities for improving care [42, 43]. These may have helped its units build the skills to improve care well, even with just an online quality-improvement tool, without a central, more expensive team of improvement coaches. The same may not be true for other healthcare organizations.

Context is a vital part of the science of improving care [44]. Future studies may therefore consider producing evidence that holds up across different organizations and networks, and across their many different circumstances. QI collaboratives or hubs, which are groups of organizations that work together on quality improvement, might help fairly build the skills to develop and test ways of improving care across organizations that deliver care [45]. This includes hubs paid for from outside.

Our review included studies of many different designs. RCTs can give the highest level of evidence when they are well done. But we also included a wider range of designs, to reflect how improvement activities and their testing actually happen in the real world, including practical limits [46]. We recorded the weaknesses of each study's design in our judgment of its risk of bias, especially among the single-center studies on discharge support.

There were also practical limits in delivering some of the programs being tested. For example, a patient teaching program led by a pharmacist was offered only to patients who were discharged during certain hours [32]. In the same way, a reengineered discharge program was limited to a set number of patients per day, chosen by nurses as "complex" cases [16]. Limits like these may affect how faithfully the programs were carried out and how accurate the results are. They may also reflect a limited budget or other limits, such as staff or in-house skills in improving or researching care, that affect how improvement activities are carried out or tested [46].

One paper used an extra measure of patient experience, called a percentile rank. This ranks each provider against its peers, showing how it performed compared with others. Only one paper used this measure, and it compared results before and after a change. It found mixed results for percentile ranks, but positive results for the percentage of top-box scores, which is the share of patients who gave the highest possible rating [31]. Reporting results in more than one way can be important, especially for percentile ranks in studies that compare before and after. This is because percentile ranks take into account how other providers perform. That partly makes up for not having a control group, or for using an older control group from the past. Overall, including studies of different designs, programs and ways of measuring patient experience may help guide future improvement activities and how they are studied.

Across the different study designs, we found some common approaches. These included extra support for coaching on care coordination [36, 37] and approaches tailored to groups of patients at risk [34, 35, 38, 40]. These often gave mixed results for patients' experiences compared with standard support. Reengineered discharge and teach back were also common approaches for discharge support. However, they gave less favorable results than studies and reviews on other outcomes, such as reducing readmissions (patients being sent back to hospital within a short time) [47–49]. For example, one recent systematic review of teach back used in discharge teaching found a 45% reduction in readmissions within 30 days [49].

For patients' experiences of care, studies using teach back had mixed results overall [28, 29, 31, 33]. In the RCTs, the results were neutral [28, 29]. This was true when teach back was the main approach [28], and when it was part of a program that combined several approaches [29]. That combined program also included a reengineered discharge, motivational interviewing (a way of talking that helps people find their own reasons to change), follow-up and help moving between care settings, and support in the patient's own language. When teach back did work better than the comparison program, it was used on its own and specifically improved patients' experiences of receiving information about new medicines [33]. For support after discharge, a program that combined several approaches, including teach back, found neutral results [29]. A program that used teach back alone found positive results on five items about patients' experiences [32]. Further research could compare how much value each approach gives for its cost, for programs that combine several approaches and for programs that use a single method. It could also find out whether combined programs, because they are complex, are carried out faithfully, keeping the main active ingredients of the program [50, 51].

To make a real difference to patients' experiences, it may be key for studies to check how patient-centered the care was. This includes how attentive, respectful, responsive and genuinely interested the care was. This could apply to teach back, to transitional support by telephone, and to other supportive communication between patients and providers. It might also include how well the communication was tailored to each individual patient [18], so that patients do not see it as just another box-ticking exercise [52].

The only study of transitional support, a practical trial of a navigator program, did not show that it worked better than usual care, although it may have had particular advantages for patients without insurance [41]. Like other kinds of complex programs, studies of transitional care may benefit from being carried out more faithfully. They may also benefit from being adapted to patients' new or particular needs and preferences, rather than following a one-size-fits-all approach [41, 53, 54]. In addition, we need measures tailored to patients' experiences of care that include the transitional support given at home [55, 56].

All the studies we included took place in the US, and there may be several reasons for this. First, the US has the CAHPS program, which provides well-established, widely used standardized measures of patients' experiences. We required studies to use these measures to be included. Second, providers' scores on CAHPS measures are reported publicly and are used in some value-based purchasing programs, which pay providers based on quality [11]. This may have encouraged providers to develop and report these improvement activities. Third, CAHPS has been a main quality target for a "person-centered" medical home. The National Committee for Quality Assurance recommended using the CAHPS survey for Patient-Centered Medical Homes to guide their change, and a related study found that CAHPS surveys were seen as useful for guiding that change [57]. Fourth, the VHA in the US has its own system for measuring patients' experiences, and it was used as a standardized measure in the studies we included [35, 36]. Fifth, improvement activities in other countries that would have met our rules for inclusion may have been carried out but not reported in English or in journals that other scientists check before publication.

In summary, the studies on how improvement activities for care coordination, discharge support and care transitions affect patients' experiences gave mixed results, and the results often cannot be applied more widely. To build on this knowledge, future work might include studies across different organizations, studies that use control groups, carrying out programs more faithfully, and making patients' experiences a more central part of what studies measure.

Limitations

Our review has several limitations. First, we left out articles published in languages other than English and articles in the grey literature, meaning reports not published in scientific journals. This affects how well the review represents the full range of research, but it means we focused on peer-reviewed knowledge that is easy for an international audience to find. Second, leaving out articles published before 2015 also affects how well the review represents the full range of research. Third, when we took information from the studies, the second reviewer only checked the work, while two reviewers worked independently on all other tasks. Fourth, we did not formally grade the strength of the evidence or the risks of bias, either within or across types of study, across very different ways of delivering care, programs and study methods. Fifth, we did not include studies that measured patients' experiences as a secondary result. Including these studies might have added to the evidence, but it would have risked including studies where improving patients' experiences of care was not a main goal.
